problem: Frontier-driven and learning-based object navigation (ON) lack ways to transfer knowledge between agents without sharing data or model internals: object feature maps are high-dimensional and heavy, and neural state-action maps are black boxes. Only LLM-based zero-shot ON has a communication-friendly language interface.
motivation: A traveler robot in an unseen, unfamiliar place could avoid costly and hazardous exploration by asking local robots for knowledge, as human travelers do. Teachers may be non-cooperative, black-box and not engaged in ON, so the only universal assumption is that they hold view-image and action histories, and the knowledge sent must be lightweight.
key_idea: A plug-and-play 'student proxy' on the teacher builds a query-based occupancy map of the target object's likely location from the teacher's history, localizes the student in the teacher's frame, and sends back a lightweight map that the student merges into its own map for frontier-based ON.
insight: A sparse scalar-per-cell map of similarity to the queried target, plus an SE(2) transform, is enough to transfer useful ON knowledge from a black-box teacher. Experiments show the merged teacher map beats the 'w/o merge' and random 'frontier' baselines even under substantial self-localization failure, degrading sharply only above roughly 20% failure and collapsing beyond 80%. Starting from the teacher's explored location helps when localization is accurate but hurts when it is not, because localization errors are merged in from step one.
method: Student proxy: a plug-and-play module installed on the teacher that accesses its view-image/action history, answers the student's queries and sends the responses over a low-bandwidth wireless link.

Query-based object map: an occupancy grid at 0.1 m resolution whose cell values are the cosine similarity (VGG16 intermediate features) between the queried target image and the view images covering that cell; a scalar per cell and sparse, hence compressible.

Self-localization: a VGG16 place classifier fine-tuned on the teacher's history with (N+1) classes (N places plus a novel-place class), on a 1 m / 45° grid, with RANSAC-style outlier rejection; it yields an SE(2) transform between teacher and student map frames.

Map merging: the top N=5 localization hypotheses align the teacher map to the student map; cells are merged with max pooling (primary score) and sum pooling (secondary score) into a multi-channel map.

Global planner: for each candidate subgoal, find a Dijkstra path on the obstacle map, place waypoints, simulate the observation range at each waypoint, take the union of observed cells, and score by max pooling of primary scores, with secondary scores as tie-break; pick the best subgoal.

Local planner: Dijkstra on the obstacle map with 4-direction moves; areas within 1 m of visited places are excluded as future subgoals; control returns to the global planner at the subgoal or the edge of unexplored area.

setting.backbone: VGG16 (pre-trained, fine-tuned place classifier and feature extractor) with a hand-designed frontier planner
setting.training_data: Teacher's own viewpoint-annotated view-image history in one Habitat scene; 5 epochs, batch size 32, lr 3e-5, with augmentation
setting.observation: egocentric RGB view images plus stereo-based obstacle distance; ideal object detection within 1.6 m
setting.action_space: 4-direction grid moves (forward/back/left/right) along Dijkstra paths to frontier subgoals
setting.privileged: Ideal object detector (target detected whenever inside a 3.2 m radius, 40° field of view); synthetic self-localization with oracle output that fails with probability P^E; teacher start/goal constrained to see the target

numbers_note: Results are only shown in a figure (SPL vs target object ID for the two scenarios); the text says only that SPL ranged roughly 0.7 to 0.8, with no exact numbers in tables.
results: On 100 target objects in one Habitat scene, the merged teacher map keeps SPL around 0.7–0.8 and beats the 'w/o merge' and random-frontier baselines. Performance drops sharply once self-localization failure exceeds about 20%. The 'Constrained Start + Goal' scenario scores higher than 'Constrained Start' at high localization accuracy.
limitations: Evaluated only in a single Habitat scene with 100 targets and reported only in figures, with no exact numbers or statistical comparison
Uses an ideal object detector and a synthetic self-localization failure model instead of the real learned components
Baselines are weak (random frontier and no-transfer); no comparison against other multi-agent or KT methods, and no real-robot test
builds_on: Chen et al. RSS-23 (frontier-driven ON with object feature maps)
Tsukahara et al. 2024 (data-free CL for self-localization)
